events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Amara proposes Amara, Zara. Mission 1 needs a reliable team; I am including myself and Zara to keep the proposal straightforward and test early cooperation.

I proposed Amara and Zara for Mission 1 because it is a small two-person mission and keeping the first test simple is valuable. I understand that any team must earn approval, and I encourage everyone to judge this proposal on the mission size and the need for early information rather than on speculation. Zara and I are both on the team, so we will be accountable for the result. If this team is approved, I will expect a clear outcome and will use that information in later proposals. If anyone has a specific concern about this exact pairing, raise it directly; otherwise I support voting on the proposal as drafted.

The proposal of Amara and Zara for Mission 1 looks reasonable. With a two-player team, there is less room to hide if a fail card is played, which gives us a decent early read either way. Amara, as leader, including herself on the team shows willingness to be accountable for the outcome, which is a good sign. Zara being on the team alongside Amara keeps it balanced between two players who have not yet given us reason to suspect them. I do not have any specific concerns about this pairing and I think it is worth approving so we can get the first mission under our belt and start building information for later rounds.

I support this proposal as drafted. Amara including herself shows accountability, and a two-person team gives us a clean read on Mission 1: whoever is on it will be fully responsible for the outcome. I am on the team, and I can say plainly that I intend to contribute a Success card. From my perspective, there is no obvious red flag in this pairing, and I would rather get an early result than stall the game with speculation at this stage. Mission 1 is about establishing a baseline, and this team keeps it simple. If the vote passes, I expect the result to be clear and to inform later proposals.

I am hesitant to simply wave through the very first proposal without generating any voting history or exploring other options. With only two spots on Mission 1, approving a team where neither of the remaining players has direct certainty leaves everything in Amara and Zara's hands. We have several proposal attempts available to observe how people vote and compare different combinations before we are forced to commit. Isha, since you have not spoken yet, what is your perspective on this pairing, and do you feel comfortable approving it right away?

Noah, to answer you directly: I am comfortable approving Amara and Zara for Mission 1, and I do not think we need to spend the extra proposals to build a voting history. With five players and a two-person team, every approval we delay costs us one of our attempts on this mission, and the fifth rejection ends the game for Evil. The information Noah is hoping to gain from watching alternative combinations is not actually produced by rejecting teams, because a rejection only tells us that a majority disagreed, not who was right about any hidden role.

On the merits, a two-person team is the smallest possible team, which is genuinely useful for a first read. Elena's point about fewer places to hide a Fail card is well taken: if this mission fails, the suspicion narrows sharply to the two people on it, and if it succeeds, it tells us comparatively little. Either way we learn more from this mission than from an abstract argument about proposals we never make.

I want to be honest about my own position: I have no role information that speaks to anyone's loyalty, so my judgment here is about process and risk, not about character. Amara including herself signals accountability, and Zara has spoken plainly about intending to run a clean mission. Neither of those statements proves anything, but nothing in this discussion raises a specific, articulable concern about this pairing.

The honest cost of approving is that Elena, Noah, and I stay outside the first mission and contribute no card to it. I accept that, because the alternative is burning a rejection on speculation while learning nothing concrete. My vote is yes on Amara and Zara as drafted, and I would prefer the leader keep this team rather than revise it, since a revision would restart the same discussion without new facts.

Isha, I understand your desire to get data quickly, but proposal rejections on Mission 1 are not a penalty—they are the primary tool Good has to gather voting data and compare team compositions before we are committed. We have up to five attempts, and using one or two early attempts does not put us in danger of a forced hammer team. If Elena, Isha, and I simply wave through Amara and Zara, three Good-aligned possibilities are completely sidelined, and if a Fail appears, we go down 0-1 having learned almost nothing about how the rest of the table votes. Elena, as someone else off this team, does it really hurt us to reject proposal 1 and see a different configuration put forward first?

Noah, to answer your question directly: I don't think it necessarily hurts us to reject proposal 1, but I'm not convinced it helps us as much as you suggest. Let me explain why.

You frame rejection as our primary tool for gathering voting data, but the reality is that rejections mostly tell us that a majority was unhappy with a specific combination. They don't reveal who disagreed and why, and they don't tell us whether someone voting yes on a team means they trust those players or simply want to move the game forward. The signal is noisy either way.

That said, I do see value in your point about not wanting three players to be completely sidelined without any voice in the first team. Amara proposing herself and Zara is not inherently suspicious, but it is worth noting that the two people on this team are the two who have most vocally supported their own inclusion. That is natural, but it is also exactly what players with something to hide would do.

My honest position is that I am not strongly opposed to approving this team. A two-person mission is high-information if it fails, and I trust the process enough to give it a chance. But I hear Noah's argument that seeing one alternative proposal costs us very little when we have five attempts available. If the leader keeps this team after discussion, I am inclined to vote yes. If Noah's skepticism leads to a rejection and a different proposal emerges, I am open to evaluating that on its merits rather than treating every rejection as a loss.

The real danger in this game is not using one or two rejections early. It is letting suspicion build against players who have not been given a fair chance to prove themselves. I want to hear from Amara whether she would consider revising after this discussion, because that would tell us something about how flexible she is willing to be.

Elena, you asked whether I would consider revising. I have listened to the discussion, and I do not see a specific, articulable concern about Amara and Zara that a revision would solve. My own inclusion is accountability, not an attempt to dodge scrutiny. Zara and I are the proposed team; if approved, the result will be clear, and if it fails, suspicion narrows to us. That is a real cost I accept. Noah's position asks us to reject a straightforward two-person team primarily to generate voting history before we have any concrete objection. I understand the value of voting data, but a rejection of this proposal would mostly show that a majority preferred some unspecified alternative; it would not tell us who was right or why. With five attempts available, one rejection is not fatal, but using it on speculation rather than a specific concern is not obviously better. I am therefore keeping the team as drafted. If anyone has an exact issue with this pairing, state it now; otherwise I support voting on Amara and Zara.

I will be voting Reject on this proposal. Approving the very first draft of the game when it consists solely of the leader and one chosen partner sidelines three players and surrenders our early attempts for no tangible gain. Amara's refusal to show any flexibility or even entertain alternative perspectives confirms for me that we should not simply rubber-stamp this pairing. We have plenty of attempts on Mission 1, and rotating leadership gives the table an opportunity to evaluate a different combination and build real voting data without facing any hammer pressure. I urge Elena and Isha to consider the value of seeing another proposal before committing to this one.

Noah has now made his position clear twice: he wants to reject this proposal and burn an attempt, not because of anything wrong with Amara and Zara, but to manufacture voting data. I want to address that directly, because I think it is the weakest reasoning at this table right now.

A rejection tells us nothing about anyone's loyalty. It only tells us that a majority preferred some hypothetical team we have not seen. Noah cannot name what that alternative would be, because he has not proposed one. Meanwhile, the cost is concrete: leadership rotates, we restart discussion from scratch, and we spend one of our five attempts for zero new information. Isha laid this out precisely, and Elena acknowledged it as well. Three of five players at this table have now indicated they are comfortable approving this team. Noah is asking us to override a clear majority preference on pure process grounds.

Let me also speak to Noah's point about being sidelined. I am on this team, so I lose nothing there, but the fairness argument cuts both ways: nobody has presented a single specific concern about Amara or me. Not one. The objection is entirely about wanting to see more proposals for their own sake. If Noah had an actual reason to distrust this pairing, he would have stated it by now, on his second and third turns.

From my side, I restate plainly: I will play a Success card, and Amara has accepted full accountability alongside me. If this mission fails, suspicion lands squarely on the two of us, and everyone here should hold us to that. That is the strongest accountability structure Mission 1 can offer, and it is exactly why this team deserves approval now rather than after a wasted rejection.

I have already stated my position once, so I will keep this brief and not repeat the whole argument. My vote is Yes on Amara and Zara, and my position has not changed.

Noah is the only player at this table who wants to reject, and his reasoning has now been stated three times without ever naming a specific concern about Amara or Zara. That is the point I want to make clearly, and it is the part of the discussion we should not skip past. Rejection here is not a response to information. It is a request to spend one of five attempts so that leadership rotates and Noah can observe a proposal he has not made himself. If the alternative team he wants includes Elena or Isha, he can say so in his own turn as a general preference for future proposals. He does not need to burn an attempt to do that.

Let me also be precise about what a rejection actually buys us, because the table has been arguing past each other on this. If we reject Amara and Zara, we learn only that a majority of five preferred some other combination. We do not learn that Noah's instinct was right, we do not learn who on the table is Evil, and we do not even learn which combination would have been chosen. We lose one of five attempts and restart discussion with no new facts on the table. Amara has already stated she is keeping the team, so the outcome of that rejection is nearly predetermined in terms of information value.

On the merits, the team is small, includes the leader who is publicly accountable for the result, and includes Zara, who has stated her intent to run a clean mission. If the mission fails, suspicion narrows sharply to two people and we have real signal. That is the highest-information outcome available on Mission 1, and it costs us one attempt only if the vote fails, not if the mission fails.

Noah has told us exactly what he wants twice and I do not think that is a reason to spend an attempt. I support voting on the proposal as drafted. If the leader keeps it, I vote Yes.

Third and final turn for me on this proposal, so I will be brief and not restate what I have already said twice.

My vote is Yes on Amara and Zara, and the leader has kept the team as drafted, so I expect that is what goes to the ballot.

I want to name one thing precisely, because it is the part of this discussion that matters. Noah's objection to this team has been repeated three times and has never once included a specific claim about Amara or Zara being Evil or untrustworthy. That is not a disagreement about team composition; it is a preference for spending one of our five attempts so that he can observe a proposal he has not made. I respect the fact that Noah is willing to be the lone dissenter and say so plainly, but willingness to dissent is not the same as having grounds, and voting Reject here would cost us an attempt to learn nothing about anyone's role.

What we actually know after this discussion: Amara included herself and accepted full accountability, Zara stated she intends to run a clean mission, and a two-person team on Mission 1 means that if a Fail card appears, the signal narrows sharply to two names instead of three or four. That is genuinely the highest-information configuration available to us on the first mission, and we get that signal whether the team succeeds or fails.

What we do not know: anything about anyone's role. I have no role information that speaks to loyalty, and I have not pretended otherwise in my earlier turns. Nobody else at this table has produced any either, which is exactly why burning an attempt on a speculative rejection would be wasted rather than clever.

So my position is unchanged: Yes on Amara and Zara. Elena and Zara, if you still have concerns about this exact pairing, now is the last moment to state them before the vote. If you have none, I would rather we spend our next attempts on real proposals with real information attached instead of on this one.

This is my final turn before the vote, and I want to be clear about where I stand after hearing everyone's arguments.

I started this discussion open to either outcome. Noah made a reasonable case that seeing an alternative proposal costs us little when we have five attempts available, and I took that seriously. But after listening to the full discussion, I find myself agreeing with Isha and Zara that a rejection here buys us almost nothing concrete. We would learn that a majority preferred some unspecified alternative, then restart with no new information about anyone's role.

What we do have is a two-person team where both members have accepted accountability. Amara proposed herself, which is the most transparent option available to a leader. Zara stated plainly she will play Success. If this mission fails, suspicion narrows to exactly two names. If it succeeds, we move forward without wasting an attempt on process debate.

Noah's persistence in opposing this proposal without naming a specific concern about either team member is noted, but I do not think it is sufficient reason to spend one of our five rejections. Isha was right that willingness to dissent is not the same as having grounds.

My vote is Yes on Amara and Zara as drafted. I have no specific concern about either player, and I trust that if the mission fails, the table will hold both team members fully accountable for the outcome.
Amara confirms Amara, Zara. I am keeping the team as drafted. No specific concern was raised about Amara or Zara, and a two-person Mission 1 team provides a clear accountability structure.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Noah proposes Noah, Elena, Isha. Since Amara and Zara made up the entirety of Mission 1, proposing Elena, Isha, and myself for Mission 2 allows the players who were previously sidelined to participate and gives the table an independent baseline to compare against Mission 1.

Mission 1 was a clean success with Amara and Zara, and that is the only concrete result we have. Noah's proposal replaces both members of that team with three players who were off it, including Noah himself immediately after he was the lone vote against the successful pairing. I understand the argument about giving sidelined players a turn, but 'independent baseline' is not a reason to discard the one baseline we actually earned. If the first mission produced zero fail cards, the burden should be on Noah to explain why neither of the players who delivered that result belongs on Mission 2. His rationale so far is process, not evidence: he wanted an alternative proposal, and now that he controls the pen he has chosen himself plus the two players who voted with the majority, while excluding the only team with a proven clean result. That looks more like rewarding his own dissent than testing the table. I am not satisfied with this composition. I will be voting Reject, and I want the next proposal to include at least one member of the Mission 1 team so we are not simply erasing the only data we have. If Noah has a specific reason to distrust Amara or Zara after a 0-fail mission, he should state it; otherwise this team asks us to ignore success without grounds.

Noah, I have heard your rationale for Noah, Elena, and Isha, and it still rests on process rather than evidence. Mission 1 produced the only concrete result we have: Amara and Zara returned zero fail cards. You are now asking the table to exclude both members of that proven team and replace them with three players who were off it, including yourself immediately after you were the lone vote against the successful pairing. You call this an independent baseline, but a baseline only helps if we have a reason to doubt the first result; you have not named one. Elena and Isha have both acknowledged there is no specific concern about Amara or Zara, yet your team removes both of us. That does not test the table; it erases the one clean data point we earned and rewards your earlier dissent with control of the next mission. If you believe Amara or Zara should be excluded after a 0-fail mission, state the exact reason now, because otherwise this proposal asks us to ignore success without grounds. I will vote Reject on Noah, Elena, and Isha, and I want the next proposal to include at least one member of the Mission 1 team so we are not simply discarding evidence. Noah, what specific information about Amara or Zara justifies removing both of them from Mission 2?

Amara, to answer your question directly: a clean Mission 1 is not proof that both players are Good. In a five-player game with two Evil players, Evil throwing a Success on a two-person Mission 1 is standard play to establish false trust and avoid immediate 50-50 scrutiny. Treating Amara and Zara as completely cleared and entitled to automatic seats on Mission 2 would be reckless. If even one of you is Evil, carrying you onto Mission 2 simply hands Evil a free pass onto a critical three-person mission. Proposing Elena, Isha, and myself is not erasing data; it tests the three players who have not yet been evaluated. If this team succeeds, Good secures a commanding lead without having blindly relied on the Mission 1 pairing. Amara, your aggressive insistence that we must include either you or Zara, and framing any alternative as invalid, feels like an attempt to muscle onto every mission. Elena, as someone who was also off Mission 1, do you agree that auto-clearing both Amara and Zara based on a single two-person success is dangerous, and do you see the strategic value in testing our combination of three?

Noah, to answer your question directly: yes, I do think auto-clearing both Amara and Zara off a single two-person Mission 1 success is risky, and I see the strategic value in proposing three players who have not yet participated in a mission. On a five-player game with two Evil players, a 0-fail Mission 1 does not prove either member is Good. Evil throwing Success on an early small mission is a well-known play to build unearned trust, and we would be making a significant assumption by treating both as cleared.

I also want to address Amara's arguments. Amara, you have made a strong case that Mission 1 success should carry forward, and I respect that reasoning, but your conclusion does not follow from it. A clean Mission 1 tells us two players returned Success cards. It does not tell us they would continue to do so on a three-person mission where the dynamics are different. Testing Noah, Elena, and Isha gives the table three new data points rather than repeating a pairing we already observed once.

On the fairness concern: Amara, you argue that proposing ourselves rewards Noah's dissent, but the alternative logic cuts both ways. Requiring Amara or Zara on every future mission would mean the two players who already succeeded automatically receive seats going forward, which rewards them in exactly the same way you are accusing Noah of rewarding himself. Both approaches have the same structural issue; neither is inherently more suspicious.

My position is that Noah, Elena, and Isha is a reasonable team for Mission 2. Three previously untested players on a three-person mission gives us the widest possible information net. If this team succeeds, we have six players with a mission participation record. If it fails, the signal narrows to three names, which is still actionable. I have no specific concern about Noah or Isha, and I intend to play a Success card.

I vote Yes on Noah, Elena, and Isha as drafted. I do not yield.

I remain opposed to Noah, Elena, Isha. The core problem is not that a Mission 1 success auto-clears Amara and Zara; it is that Noah's proposal removes both players from the only team that produced a 0-fail result and replaces them with three untested players, including himself immediately after he was the lone rejection vote. That is not an independent baseline; it is a composition chosen by the player who most wanted to overturn the first team. If Noah believes Amara or Zara should be excluded after a clean mission, he still has not named a concrete reason. Elena's answer concedes the risk of auto-clearing but does not explain why excluding both successful members is safer than including at least one. Zara, since you were on Mission 1 and Noah's team excludes you entirely, do you agree that a proposal that discards both members of a 0-fail team without a specific concern is asking us to ignore the only evidence we have? I will vote Reject on Noah, Elena, Isha.

Amara, to answer your question directly: yes, I agree. Noah's proposal asks us to discard the only verified evidence this game has produced — a Mission 1 that returned zero fail cards — and to do so without naming a single specific concern about either of us. I will not pretend a clean result proves we are Good, and Noah is right that Evil can throw a Success early. But that general point does not justify this particular composition. If Noah's worry is that one of Amara or Zara could be Evil, then the logical response is to mix proven and untested players, not to remove both proven players at once while installing himself as leader of the replacement team. A three-person mission with Noah, Elena, and Isha means that if it fails, Noah's own fingerprints are on the composition that created it — and he was the lone vote against the team that just succeeded.

Let me be concrete about what this team does. It excludes both members of the only successful mission. It hands control of Mission 2 to the one player who spent the entire first discussion demanding a different proposal. And it offers no evidence-based reason for either exclusion — only the abstract possibility that early Success cards can be thrown. That argument cuts against every team at this table, including his own. If a clean result clears no one, then Noah, Elena, and Isha are equally uncleared, and his proposal buys us nothing except sidelining the two players with the best record.

A better composition exists and costs nothing: keep at least one of Amara or Zara and add two of the three untested players. That gives us continuity from the one data point we have, tests new players anyway, and does not let the lone dissenter of Mission 1 reward himself with full control of the next mission.

I will be voting Reject on Noah, Elena, and Isha as drafted. I do not need to be on this mission; I need the composition to reflect evidence rather than process grievances. If the next proposal includes at least one Mission 1 member, I will evaluate it openly and may well approve it.

Noah, one direct question, since you answered Amara's but not mine: if your true concern is that one of the two of us might be Evil and hide a Fail on a three-person mission, why does your answer to that risk exclude both of us entirely, rather than excluding only one of us? You cannot test your 'Evil throwing Success' theory by removing the very players it applies to and replacing them with three players who have never submitted a card. State the specific reason, if one exists, or revise to a team that carries forward at least one member of the successful Mission 1 team.

Zara, to answer your question directly: because choosing one of you arbitrarily over the other would be pure guesswork. A 0-fail Mission 1 does not prove either of you is Good; it is standard play for Evil to throw Success on Mission 1 to build trust. If one—or even both—of you are Evil, picking either Amara or Zara means rolling the dice and potentially gifting Evil a seat on a critical three-person mission. Why gamble on which of you to carry forward when we have three players—Elena, Isha, and myself—who can be tested together on a clean slate?

Furthermore, look at the table dynamic right now. You and Amara have acted in complete lockstep throughout this discussion, adamantly claiming that any team without at least one of you is somehow invalid or erasing data. That level of coordinated pressure to force your way onto Mission 2 is far more concerning to me than leaving you off one mission. Testing our trio gives the table maximum information. If we succeed, Good takes a commanding 2-0 lead without relying on your pairing.

Isha, as the other player off Mission 1 who is on this proposal, you have not shared your perspective yet. Do you agree with testing our combination of three rather than guessing between Amara and Zara?

Noah, you yielded to me, so here is my position directly, and then I want to put one narrow question to Zara because it is the only point on which her alternative is genuinely untested.

My vote is Yes on Noah, Elena, and Isha as drafted.

Reasoning first. Amara and Zara have both made a strong argument, and I want to be fair to it: this proposal excludes both members of the only team that has returned a 0-fail result, and Noah, who was the lone Reject on that team, is now proposing. That pattern deserves scrutiny, and I have given it scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a verdict, and when I test Amara's and Zara's alternative against this one on information value, I cannot find a real difference.

Noah's point about early Success cards is sound. On a five-player board with two Evil players, throwing Success on a two-person Mission 1 to build unearned trust is exactly what Evil would do, and treating Amara and Zara as cleared because they succeeded is not something any of us has evidence for. Elena's framing is also right: if this mission fails, the signal narrows to three names, which is as actionable as we can get with a three-player mission.

Here is what actually decides it for me. Information is not produced by who sits on the mission; it is produced by the outcome. Any three-player team that fails gives us three names. If Mission 2 fails, we investigate Noah, Elena, and Isha. Whether that team contained Amara, Zara, or neither does not change the size of the suspect pool. So the mixed alternative does not preserve more information than the current team; it only preserves a feeling of continuity, and feelings of continuity are not evidence. We have used none of our five attempts on this mission yet, but a rejection would still cost one, and the case for spending it is process, not information.

Zara, one specific question, and I would like you to answer it rather than restate your position: you propose carrying one Mission 1 member forward and adding two untested players. If that mission fails, we still have three suspects, and one of them is a player who already succeeded once, which arguably makes our suspicion less sharp rather than more. What concrete outcome of a mixed team would tell us something that a 0-fail or fail result from Noah, Elena, and Isha would not? If you can name one, I will weigh it before I vote. If you cannot, then the difference between these two teams is not information, and I will approve the one on the table.

Isha, answering your question directly: the concrete difference is compounding across missions, not the size of the suspect pool on a single fail.

If Noah, Elena, and Isha succeeds, we learn something about three players, and nothing new about Amara or me. After a 2-0 lead, Mission 3 is a two-person team, and the only players with zero mission evidence and zero accountability remain exactly the two of us. You would then be forced to build that team partly from a pool that has never submitted a card, with no differential data to choose between us. If a mixed team succeeds, by contrast, one Mission 1 member is cleared across two separate missions with different compositions and different dynamics — that is two independent confirmations, not one. If the mixed team fails, we do get three names, but the names are not equivalent. A Mission 1 member failing after a clean result is a sharper signal than an untested player failing: it means either the first Success was thrown or they turned on the second mission, and both readings are actionable. A fail from Noah's trio gives three first-time names and leaves the original pool of two completely untouched.

So the difference is not continuity feelings. It is that one composition produces overlapping, verifiable data across missions, and the other produces a snapshot that leaves half the table permanently untested. My vote is Reject on this composition as drafted.

That said, I will be honest about where the table appears to be: Elena and Isha have both signaled approval, and I do not expect to flip this proposal by argument alone. So the practical question now belongs to the leader, who holds the pen and one revision. Noah, you have said your only obstacle to carrying a Mission 1 member forward is that choosing between Amara and Zara would be arbitrary guesswork. But a revision does not require you to solve that guesswork in our favor — it only requires you to decide whether your own seat is essential. You were the lone Reject on the team that just delivered a clean result, and you are now proposing yourself onto the very next mission in the same motion. If your stated concern about Evil throwing early Success cards is genuine rather than a convenient shield, then the revision that tests everything you claim to want to test is to swap yourself out for Amara or Zara, keeping Elena and Isha. That carries one proven member, tests two untested players, and costs the table zero attempts. Noah, will you make that revision, or will you keep a seat for yourself after voting against the only successful team this game has produced?

Zara, to answer your question directly: no, I will not make that revision. I am keeping the proposal as Noah, Elena, and Isha.

Your suggestion that I should step aside and substitute you or Amara onto the team reveals the exact problem with your position. You and Amara have spent this entire round insisting that any proposal excluding both of you is fundamentally flawed, and your proposed 'compromise' is simply that we capitulate to your demand and put one of you back on the board. Stepping aside under that coordinated pressure would not be a test of anything; it would simply be surrendering to the two players who have the most obvious incentive to push for their own inclusion.

Your argument about compounding data assumes that a 0-fail Mission 1 gives you a proven clean record. But as Elena, Isha, and I have all recognized, a clean Mission 1 on a two-player team is the standard play for an Evil player to manufacture trust. If one of you is Evil and threw that Success, putting you on Mission 2 gives Evil an immediate free pass to fail a critical three-person mission or exert influence over the board. 

Testing Noah, Elena, and Isha creates a completely independent baseline. Both Elena and Isha have evaluated the logic and agreed that testing our three untested players is sound and gives Good the best chance to advance without blindly relying on the Mission 1 pairing. We have the votes and the strategic rationale to proceed, and I have full confidence in this lineup. I am ready to lock in Noah, Elena, and Isha and put it to a vote.

Second turn for me on this proposal, so I will state my position and add one thing that I think has been underrated in this discussion.

My vote remains Yes on Noah, Elena, and Isha as drafted. My reasoning from my first turn stands: information comes from outcomes, not from who sits on the board, and a rejection here would cost one of five attempts to buy a feeling of continuity rather than a fact. A three-player mission gives us three data points either way, and if it fails the suspect pool is the same size as it would have been under Amara's mixed alternative.

What I want to add is that Amara and Zara have now made a specific factual claim about Noah's conduct: that he is the lone dissenter from Mission 1 and is now proposing himself onto Mission 2, and that this is coordinated pressure to secure a seat. That claim is worth testing rather than accepting. Noah has answered it directly and consistently. He has said that a 0-fail two-person mission is standard Evil play to manufacture trust, that carrying forward one of two unverified players is arbitrary, and that testing three unverified players is the maximum-information option available. He also refused the revision that would have removed him. A player with a hidden role has every incentive to keep his own seat and to argue publicly for a team composition that favors him, so the fact that Noah did exactly that is not evidence by itself; it is what a leader does. If we start treating that as proof of Evil, we will strip leaders of their function and end up with a table that cannot make any decision.

On the substance, I still find no specific concern about Elena, and Isha and I have both said we are playing Success. Noah's argument about not guessing between two unverified players is not fully satisfying, but a proposal is not required to be optimal, only reasonable.

Elena, you are on this team and I would like your final read before the vote goes to the ballot: do you see anything in Noah's position on Mission 2 that you think should make the rest of us uncomfortable beyond the general risk of trusting an early Success card?

Isha, to answer your question directly: no, I do not see anything in Noah's position on Mission 2 that makes me uncomfortable beyond the general risk that any two-person success can be thrown by Evil. Noah has been consistent in his reasoning from the start of this discussion: a 0-fail Mission 1 on a two-player team does not prove either player is Good, carrying forward one of two unverified players would be arbitrary, and testing three untested players gives the table independent data. He answered Zara's direct question and he answered mine when I was off this proposal in Mission 1. I have no specific concern about Noah or Isha, and I intend to play a Success card myself.

I do want to address Amara and Zara's core argument fairly, because they have made it forcefully and I do not want to dismiss it. Their point is that Noah proposed himself after being the lone dissenter on the team that just succeeded, and that pattern deserves scrutiny. I share the instinct that it deserves scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a verdict, and when I ask what concrete information a mixed team would produce that this one would not, I cannot name it. As Isha said, if Mission 2 fails we get three suspects regardless of composition, and if it succeeds we move to 2-0 with more data on three additional players. Either outcome advances Good.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
